newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Philadelphia exhibit shows Michelangelo-Rodin link.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Philadelphia exhibit shows Michelangelo-Rodin link.

text.p: In 1876, struggling French sculptor Auguste Rodin travelled to Italy and found the road to greatness.

The reason was Michelangelo, who was born four centuries earlier but whose example captivated Rodin and infused his work with a characteristic expressiveness and strength that propelled him to the top ranks of modern sculptors. Now the Philadelphia Museum of Art highlights the relationship with an exhibition that opened this week of the two artists' work entitled "Rodin and Michelangelo: A Study in Artistic Inspiration."

The show contains 13 drawings and three small sculptures by Michelangelo and 40 works of Rodin. It is accompanied by a separate exhibition of 60 sculptures highlighting Rodin's treatment of the human hand, a hallmark of his work.

The main exhibition focuses on Rodin's trip to Italy in 1876, when he saw the work of Michelangelo. Especially important were visits to the Medici Chapel in Florence, with its monumental sculptures, and, in all likelihood, Casa Buonarroti, the Michelangelo home and museum.

"To tell you that since my first hour in Florence I have been making a study of Michelangelo will not suprise you," Rodin wrote to his companion, Rose Beuret. "I believe that the great magician is giving up a few of his secrets to me."
At the time of the visit, Rodin was 35. He had failed three times to win acceptance into Paris' prestigous Ecole des Beaux-Arts and worked in obscurity.

In Italy, Rodin was exposed to the adulation of Michelangelo in the wake of celebrations a year earlier of the 400th anniversary of the Italian artist's birth and was able to study and sketch the master's works. His visit, exhibition co-curator Christopher Riopelle said, "really changed the course of his career and really gave him a sense of what he could aspire to."
The exhibition shows Rodin drawings of Michelangelo's artwork in the Medici Chapel, the Sistine Chapel and elsewhere and bronze sculptures by Rodin that clearly show Michelangelo's influence.

Riopelle said a study in the exhibit drawn by Michelangelo for his "Libyan Sibyl" on the Sistine Chapel captures a twisting, forceful torso with a dynamism later to be seen in Rodin's work. Similarly, a small wax Michelangelo sculpture called "River God" showed an angularity of pose that also was adopted by Rodin.

A white earthenware vase made around 1887 illustrates an early attempt by Rodin to draw from Michelangelo. Four seated figures at the base of the work seem to be struggling mightily to support the rim with powerful, muscled bodies.
But since Rodin was still an unknown sculptor, the vase was signed by a more prosperous artist he assisted, leaving scholars later to discern the hand of Rodin in its figures.
"This can only be the work of Rodin attempting to understand Michelangelo," Riopelle said.

Another highlight of the exhibit is Michelangelo's early study "The Last Judgment" in the Sistine Chapel. The triumphant, swirling composition of that drawing is echoed in Rodin's unfinshed bronze masterwork "The Gates of Hell."

There is even evidence Rodin's most famous work, "The Thinker" -- which is incorporated into "The Gates of Hell" -- was inspired at least in part by Michelangelo's sculpture of Lorenzo de' Medici in a similar pose, gazing pensively, from above de' Medici's tomb.

The second exhibit, "The Hands of Rodin," is from the collection of the late brokerage founder B. Gerald Cantor. It shows the sculptor's fascination with the expressive capabilities of the human hand in examples ranging from an agonized, arthritic claw to the delicate spiritual vessel formed by two elongate, cupped hands.

It also shows the power of hand gestures in full figures including the sensual touch of "The Kiss" and the resignation of one of "The Burghers of Calais," who offered his life to spare his besieged city.
